headline: Conflict is inevitable when different people with different needs interact—the question is how we handle it
universal_truth: Disagreement isn't failure; it's information; how you disagree matters more than whether you disagree
fun_facts: Research shows couples who can disagree constructively have stronger relationships than those who avoid conflict
Teams with healthy conflict produce more creative solutions than teams with false harmony
Most conflicts are about unmet needs or miscommunication, not genuine value differences
discussion_questions: How do you typically handle disagreement?
When has conflict led to something positive?
What makes some conflicts constructive and others destructive?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Wherever people gather, conflict follows. Different needs, different views, different priorities—friction is inevitable. But conflict isn't inherently bad. Some disagreements clear the air. Some lead to better ideas. The question isn't if you'll conflict, but how.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: We often try to avoid conflict, treating it as failure. But suppressed conflict doesn't disappear—it festers. What's the difference between destructive and constructive conflict?

options.text: Constructive conflict focuses on issues rather than people, seeks understanding before agreement, and aims for resolution rather than victory
options.response: Yes. Constructive conflict attacks problems, not people. It's curious before it's certain. It aims to solve, not to win. The goal is mutual understanding, even without agreement.

options.text: Constructive conflict is when you eventually agree
options.response: Agreement is nice, but constructive conflict can end with respectful disagreement...

q1.title: Issue vs Person
q1.script: Destructive conflict attacks people: 'You're wrong, you're stupid, you're bad.' Constructive conflict attacks issues: 'This approach has problems.' The same disagreement becomes either relationship-damaging or problem-solving depending on the target.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Issue vs Person"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Understand First
q2.script: Most conflicts stem from misunderstanding—assumptions about what the other person means or wants. Before arguing, seek to understand. 'What are you actually concerned about?' often dissolves apparent conflict into shared problem-solving.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Conflict Avoidance Cost
q3.script: Avoiding conflict feels peaceful but creates problems. Resentment builds. Issues go unaddressed. Passive aggression replaces honest disagreement. The short-term comfort of avoidance creates long-term dysfunction.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Disagreement isn't failure; it's information. How you disagree matters more than whether you disagree. Learn to fight well.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 203. Tomorrow, we'll explore what peace actually means. Until then, in your next disagreement, try understanding before arguing.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Conflict Practice - Understand First
growTrack.activity: In your next disagreement, before responding, ask: 'Can you help me understand your concern?' Listen without defending. Often what seems like opposition is actually a different way of looking at a shared goal.
